To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

adolescents who seriously considered but did not attempt suicide in the past 12 months were more likely than non suicidal youth to have positive help seeking attitudes, perceive that adults at school would respond to suicide, and have a willingness to overcome peer pressure to remain silent about suicide.
adolescents' attitudes about help seeking and their social environments are not associated with suicidal help seeking behavior.

adolescents who have suicidal thoughts are more likely to seek help from an adult if they perceive that adult as available and willing to help them, if they perceive that their school is a safe place where adults are willing to listen to them, and if they perceive that adults at school can help them overcome the stigma associated with suicide.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of help seeking attitudes in adolescent suicidal behavior.
the development of interventions to reduce the incidence of suicide in adolescents.
the social and cultural context of suicide, and with the ways in which social relationships and social norms shape adolescents' decisions to seek help.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the study supports that students' perceptions of adults' willingness and capability to help them and their understanding of the availability of resources to help them cope are important factors in their help seeking behaviors.
suicidal help seeking youth who disclosed SI to adults were more likely to seek help from adults if they perceived that adults would help, and they had positive attitudes about help seeking.
help seeking is a complex process that is affected by many variables.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
students who are more likely to help themselves and others are more likely to be engaged in their school and community, to have supportive relationships with adults, and to have coping skills.
the more students believe that adults can help them, the more likely they are to seek help.
students who are suicidal are more likely to seek help from adults if they perceive that adults would respond and if they have positive attitudes toward adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should not assume that adolescents who consider suicide will seek help, or that they will be able to get help if they do seek it.
we need to focus more on the attitudes, norms, and social environment that shape adolescents' help seeking behavior.

students who are suicidal are more likely to seek help if they perceive that they have a support network at school, that the school environment is safe and welcoming, and that adults at the school are available and capable to help.
